rounds.response:
Maya: A quick rule—if one distribution puts more probability on values farther from its mean (more mass at the extremes or a larger range), it will generally have a larger variance, so compare where the mass sits relative to the center instead of always summing squares.  
Jared: Submissions are normally locked after the deadline—check the course/platform late-policy and email the instructor/TA ASAP if you need to report an upload error or request a replacement.  
Linh: Your renormalization is correct; do it when you have unnormalized weights or a missing total, but don’t renormalize if the problem claims those are the final probabilities (then a sum ≠1 indicates an error or omitted outcomes to clarify).  
Omar: Here you can compute exactly—mean=0.1, only 0 and 1 are within 1 unit so P(within 1)=0.5+0.3=0.8 (80%); Chebyshev gives a weaker general bound (≥51%) if you only know variance.  
Sara: Yes—P(X≥2) = sum of the probabilities for values 2 and larger (equivalently 1 − P(X≤1) if that’s easier).
